question: What is CSRF and how does it work?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)** tricks a browser into sending an unwanted request with credentials that the browser adds automatically. A session cookie is the usual example, but HTTP Basic credentials and client certificates can also be sent automatically. The server sees valid credentials unless it checks that the request came through an allowed flow. Common defenses are a CSRF token on unsafe requests, `SameSite` cookies, origin checks, and keeping GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE free of state changes.

sections.title: What CSRF Is and Why It Works
sections.content:
**Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)** tricks a browser into sending an unwanted request to an application where the user already has credentials. The attacker normally cannot read the response, but a forged transfer, email change, or delete can still cause damage.

It works because some credentials are **ambient**: the browser adds them without code on the current page knowing their value. A session cookie is the common case. HTTP Basic credentials and client certificates can also be ambient. If a malicious page submits a request to the target site, the browser may attach those credentials and the server may accept the request as the user.

A CSRF token places an unpredictable value in a form field or request header that a cross-site page cannot normally read and replay. `SameSite` cookies and origin checks add more protection. A bearer token sent explicitly in the `Authorization` header avoids the usual CSRF mechanism, provided no other automatically sent credential can authenticate the same endpoint.

sections.title: How a CSRF Attack Unfolds
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[Victim logs into bank.com
session cookie set] --> B[Victim visits
malicious site in another tab] B --> C[Malicious page auto-submits
hidden form to bank.com/transfer] C --> D[Browser attaches bank.com
cookie automatically] D --> E{Server checks
anti-CSRF token?} E -->|No token / not validated| F[Transfer executes
as the victim] E -->|Token required + valid| G[Request rejected 403
attacker can't supply token] ```

sections.title: Vulnerable: state-changing GET / no CSRF token
Safe: POST + CSRF token (Spring Security default)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing CSRF with XSS**: XSS runs attacker-controlled script in a trusted page; CSRF sends a forged request with ambient credentials.
- **Calling it a cookie-only attack**: cookies are the usual cause, but HTTP Basic authentication and client certificates may also be sent automatically.
- **Changing state with GET**: links and embedded resources can trigger GET requests. Safe HTTP methods must not perform mutations.
- **Disabling protection because an endpoint is called REST**: the name of the API does not matter; credential transport does.
- **Believing HTTPS stops CSRF**: TLS protects the connection, not the intent of an authenticated request.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **CSRF sends an unwanted request with credentials that the browser supplies automatically.**
- Session cookies are common ambient credentials; HTTP Basic and client certificates can also matter.
- The attacker usually cannot read the response, but can still trigger a state change.
- Use **CSRF tokens** on unsafe requests, plus `SameSite` cookies and origin checks where suitable.
- A bearer token in `Authorization` avoids the usual CSRF path only when no ambient credential can authenticate the endpoint.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
CSRF is an attack in which another site causes a browser to send an unwanted request to an application where the user already has credentials. A bank-transfer form is the usual example: the malicious page submits the form, the browser adds the bank's session cookie, and the bank may see an authenticated request even though the user did not intend it.

The important condition is not JWT versus session; it is whether the browser supplies a credential automatically. Session cookies are the common case, but HTTP Basic credentials and client certificates can also be ambient. A bearer token added explicitly to the `Authorization` header is different because a normal cross-site form cannot add that header or read the token.

For a cookie-authenticated Spring application, CSRF protection should remain enabled. Spring requires an unpredictable token on unsafe requests and rejects a missing or invalid token. `SameSite` cookies and origin checks provide additional protection. Safe methods such as GET must remain read-only, because links and embedded resources can trigger them easily.

question: How does a CSRF token work?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: A CSRF token is an unpredictable value that a legitimate page sends with an unsafe request in a form field or header. The server compares it with the value expected for that user or browser. Another site may cause the browser to send cookies, but it cannot normally read the token from the protected origin, so its forged request lacks a valid token. The token can be stored in a session or another CSRF token repository; it is not required to be a new per-session value for every design.

sections.title: Why a Secret Token Defeats CSRF
sections.content:
A **CSRF token** is an unpredictable value that a legitimate page sends with an unsafe request, normally in a hidden form field or request header. The server compares it with the value expected by its CSRF token repository.

A forged cross-site form may carry the user's session cookie, but the attacking page cannot normally read the protected page or its token because of the same-origin policy. Its request therefore arrives without the valid request token and is rejected. A custom-header request also requires a CORS preflight, which the server should not allow for an untrusted origin.

The expected token may be kept in the HTTP session or in another repository. For an SPA, Spring's `CookieCsrfTokenRepository` writes a readable `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie so trusted JavaScript can copy the value into `X-XSRF-TOKEN`. The server still validates the request value; merely receiving a cookie is not enough.

sections.title: Token Validation Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[Server renders form
with hidden _csrf token] --> B[Legit page submits
cookie + matching token] B --> C{Token present
and valid?} C -->|Yes| D[Request processed] A --> E[Attacker page submits
cookie but no token] E --> F[Same-origin policy blocks
reading the real token] F --> G{Token present?} G -->|No / wrong| H[403 Forbidden
forgery blocked] ```

sections.title: Vulnerable: CSRF disabled, no token required
Safe: Spring Security CSRF token (default + SPA setup)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Sending a token only as an automatically attached cookie**: the server must validate a request field or header as well.
- **Assuming every design uses one token per session**: token storage and rotation depend on the configured repository.
- **Protecting unsafe GET handlers with a token**: GET should be read-only; do not use a token to justify side effects.
- **Disabling CSRF to remove a 403**: first fix how the legitimate client obtains and submits the token.
- **Calling it authentication**: the login credential identifies the principal; the CSRF check helps establish that an unsafe browser request followed an allowed flow.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- A CSRF token is **unpredictable** and is validated on unsafe requests.
- A legitimate page submits it through a form field or request header.
- Another origin cannot normally read the protected page's token.
- Spring can keep the expected token in a session or use `CookieCsrfTokenRepository` for cookie-to-header clients.
- A cookie alone is not the check; the server validates the submitted request value.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A CSRF token is an unpredictable value that the application expects with a state-changing browser request. A server-rendered form can include it as a hidden field. An SPA can read a CSRF cookie and copy the value into a request header. The server compares the submitted value with the token held by its configured repository.

For example, an attacker can submit a hidden form to `bank.example/transfer`; the victim's browser may attach the bank login cookie automatically. The attacker cannot normally read the bank's CSRF token, so the forged form cannot supply the required value and the server rejects the transfer.

Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default. It supports a session-backed token and `CookieCsrfTokenRepository` for SPA-style cookie-to-header handling. The important rule is that the server validates a value deliberately submitted by the legitimate client; a token that arrives only as an automatically attached cookie would not provide that check.

question: Why are stateless REST APIs with JWT not vulnerable to CSRF?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: A JWT does not prevent CSRF by itself. A browser API is normally outside the usual CSRF threat when its only credential is a bearer token that client code adds to the `Authorization` header, because the browser does not attach that header automatically. A cross-site form therefore has no credential to reuse. If the same JWT is stored in an automatically sent cookie, or another ambient credential can authenticate the endpoint, CSRF protection is still needed.

sections.title: No Ambient Cookie, No CSRF
sections.content:
CSRF relies on a credential that the browser sends **automatically**. A JWT is often sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, and the browser does not invent or attach that header on its own. A normal cross-site form therefore reaches the API without the bearer token and is rejected as unauthenticated.

JavaScript on another origin cannot read the application's token. Asking to send an `Authorization` header also triggers a CORS preflight, which the API should allow only for trusted origins. CORS is not the main CSRF defense here—the absence of an ambient credential is—but a loose CORS policy can create other cross-origin risks.

The token's **transport**, not its JWT format, decides the CSRF exposure. Put the JWT in an automatically sent cookie and the browser can carry it on a forged request, so CSRF protection is needed again. The same is true if an endpoint also accepts a session cookie, HTTP Basic credentials, or another ambient credential.

sections.title: CSRF Exposure by Token Storage
sections.content:
emerald|Bearer header only|~Usual CSRF path absent|client adds the token|cross-site form has no token|CSRF filter can be disabled for that chain
rose|JWT in cookie|~CSRF-exposed|browser may send it automatically|same risk as session cookie|keep CSRF protection
blue|CORS role|~Controls browser reads/header requests|Authorization triggers preflight|allow trusted origins only|not a replacement for authentication
amber|Decision|~Check every accepted credential|any ambient credential?|yes: protect unsafe requests|no: CSRF check may be unnecessary

sections.title: Risky: JWT in an auto-sent cookie, CSRF disabled
Safe: stateless API, token in Authorization header
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating JWT as a CSRF feature**: a JWT in a cookie is still an automatically sent credential.
- **Ignoring another authentication path**: a bearer API that also accepts a session cookie may still be exposed.
- **Calling header requests impossible cross-origin**: an `Authorization` header triggers preflight; the server's CORS policy decides whether the browser may continue.
- **Using local storage as a complete security fix**: it avoids automatic cookie sending but makes token theft through XSS a separate concern.
- **Disabling protection based only on the word REST**: inspect how every accepted credential reaches the endpoint.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **JWT is not inherently CSRF-safe**; transport is what matters.
- A bearer header is not added automatically, so a cross-site form has no credential to reuse.
- A JWT in an authentication cookie needs CSRF protection.
- Check for sessions, Basic authentication, client certificates, or other ambient credentials too.
- Disable CSRF only on a security chain where no accepted credential is automatically sent.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A stateless API is not protected from CSRF merely because its token is a JWT. The usual protection comes from sending the token as a bearer value in the `Authorization` header. The browser does not add that header automatically, so a cross-site form reaches the API without a credential and the API rejects it.

A script on another origin also needs the token and must pass a CORS preflight before the browser can send an `Authorization` header. The server should allow only trusted origins. The core point, however, is that there is no ambient credential for the attacker to reuse.

If the JWT is stored in a cookie that authenticates the request, the browser may send it automatically and CSRF is possible again. The same applies if the endpoint also accepts a session cookie, HTTP Basic authentication, or a client certificate. CSRF can be disabled for a Spring Security chain only after confirming that its accepted credentials are supplied explicitly rather than automatically.

question: What is the SameSite cookie attribute and how does it prevent CSRF?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: `SameSite` tells a browser when a cookie is eligible to accompany a cross-site request. `Strict` omits it on cross-site requests. `Lax` allows it on some top-level navigations that use a safe method, while blocking common cross-site POST and embedded-request cases. `None` permits cross-site use and requires `Secure`, although browser privacy settings may still block it. `SameSite` reduces CSRF exposure but should be treated as defense in depth rather than the only check for sensitive actions.

sections.title: Controlling When Cookies Cross Sites
sections.content:
The **`SameSite`** cookie attribute controls when a cookie is eligible to be sent with a request that begins on another **site**. This is a site-level rule, not the same as the browser's stricter origin rule. It helps against CSRF because many attacks depend on an authentication cookie accompanying a forged cross-site request.

`Strict` omits the cookie for cross-site requests. `Lax` allows it on some top-level navigations using safe methods, such as following a link, but normally omits it for cross-site POSTs and embedded requests. `None` permits cross-site use and must be combined with `Secure`; browser privacy rules can still block third-party cookies.

Modern browsers generally apply Lax-like behavior when the attribute is absent, sometimes with compatibility exceptions. Set the attribute explicitly so the intended behavior is clear. For important state changes, keep a CSRF token or another strong request-intent check as well.

sections.title: SameSite Values at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Strict|~Strong restriction|omitted on cross-site requests|inbound request may look signed out|cookie still exists
blue|Lax|~Balanced|some top-level safe navigations allowed|cross-site POST normally omitted|common session choice
rose|None|~Cross-site use allowed|requires Secure|needed for some embeds or separate sites|privacy controls may still block
amber|Security role|~Defense in depth|reduces ambient-cookie exposure|does not fix unsafe GET handlers|combine with CSRF token for sensitive writes

sections.title: Vulnerable: session cookie with no SameSite control
sections.content:
```properties
# This cookie is intentionally eligible for cross-site use.
server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=none
server.servlet.session.cookie.secure=true
```
*If this cookie authenticates state-changing requests, `SameSite=None` supplies no CSRF barrier; use a CSRF token or redesign the credential flow.*

sections.title: Safe: SameSite=Lax (or Strict) + Secure
sections.content:
```properties
# Block the session cookie on cross-site POSTs / background requests
server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=lax    # or 'strict' for sensitive apps
server.servlet.session.cookie.secure=true       # HTTPS only
server.servlet.session.cookie.http-only=true    # also blocks JS access (XSS)
```
```java
// Or set it explicitly on a custom cookie
ResponseCookie cookie = ResponseCookie.from("SESSION", value)
    .httpOnly(true).secure(true).sameSite("Lax").path("/").build();
response.addHeader(HttpHeaders.SET_COOKIE, cookie.toString());
```
*With `Lax`, a cross-site POST to your transfer endpoint won't carry the session cookie — the forged request is unauthenticated.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating SameSite as the only CSRF defense**: keep a token or equivalent check for sensitive unsafe requests.
- **Relying on an omitted attribute**: browser defaults and compatibility behavior can vary; set the intended value explicitly.
- **Using `None` without `Secure`**: modern browsers reject that combination.
- **Saying Strict logs the user out**: the cookie remains stored; it is simply omitted on the cross-site request.
- **Confusing SameSite with HttpOnly**: HttpOnly blocks JavaScript from reading the cookie, but injected script can still send authenticated requests.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `SameSite` controls cookie sending across **sites**, not origins.
- `Strict` omits the cookie cross-site; `Lax` permits some top-level safe navigations.
- `None` allows cross-site use and requires `Secure`.
- An absent attribute often gets Lax-like browser handling, but explicit configuration is clearer.
- Use SameSite as defense in depth, not permission to make GET change state.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The `SameSite` attribute tells the browser when a cookie may accompany a request that starts on another site. It helps against CSRF because a forged request is less useful when the browser withholds the authentication cookie.

With `Strict`, the cookie is omitted on cross-site requests. The cookie is not deleted, so the user is not literally logged out; the first inbound request may simply look unauthenticated. `Lax` keeps normal top-level navigation working for safe methods but normally blocks the cookie on cross-site POSTs and embedded requests. `None` permits cross-site use and requires `Secure`, although browser privacy settings may still prevent third-party cookies.

SameSite is a useful browser-side barrier, but it is defense in depth. Sensitive writes should still use a CSRF token or an equivalent request-intent check, and GET must remain read-only. The application should set SameSite explicitly rather than depend on a browser's default behavior.

question: When should you disable CSRF protection in Spring Security?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: Disable Spring Security's CSRF protection only for endpoints that cannot be authenticated by credentials the browser sends automatically. A bearer-only API commonly qualifies because the client must add its token to `Authorization`. Keep CSRF protection for session cookies, authentication cookies, HTTP Basic credentials, client certificates, and mixed chains that accept any of them. The deciding check is every authentication mechanism accepted by the endpoint, not whether it is called REST or stateless.

sections.title: The One Question That Decides It
sections.content:
Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default. Whether it can be disabled depends on **how the protected endpoint is authenticated**, not on whether the controller returns JSON.

Keep CSRF protection when a browser can authenticate the request with something it supplies automatically: a session or JWT cookie, HTTP Basic credentials, or a client certificate are common examples. For an API security chain whose only credential is a bearer token that the client explicitly adds to `Authorization`, there is normally no ambient credential for a forged request to reuse, so that chain can disable CSRF.

Inspect every accepted mechanism. A supposedly stateless API may still accept a session cookie, and a bearer endpoint may share a chain with form login. Mixed applications can use separate security chains or ignore only selected endpoints after their credential flows are understood. A CSRF 403 in a cookie application should be fixed by submitting the token, not by removing the check.

sections.title: Enable or Disable? Decide by Credential Transport
sections.content:
rose|Ambient credential accepted|~Keep CSRF|session or JWT cookie|HTTP Basic or client certificate|browser can authenticate automatically
emerald|Bearer-only chain|~Can disable|client adds Authorization|no accepted ambient credential|cross-site form arrives unauthenticated
amber|Decision scope|~Inspect the whole chain|all auth mechanisms|all matching endpoints|document the reason
blue|Mixed application|~Separate policies|browser pages keep CSRF|bearer API may disable|do not use one blanket rule

sections.title: Wrong: disabling CSRF on a cookie/session app
sections.content:
```java
// Form login uses the session cookie -> this app NEEDS CSRF protection
http.formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())
    .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable());   // BUG: opens the app to CSRF to silence 403s
```
*The session cookie is auto-sent, so disabling CSRF here makes every POST forgeable.*

sections.title: Right: disable only for stateless header-token APIs
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Disabling CSRF for all REST APIs**: JSON responses do not determine CSRF risk.
- **Checking only for cookies**: HTTP Basic and client-certificate credentials may also be sent automatically.
- **Assuming stateless means no ambient credentials**: stateless Basic authentication is still browser-supplied.
- **Removing the filter to silence 403**: in a cookie application, make the client submit the token.
- **Forgetting mixed security chains**: scope the policy to endpoints with the same credential model.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Disable CSRF only when **no accepted credential is browser-supplied automatically**.
- A bearer-only `Authorization` API can commonly disable it.
- Keep it for session/JWT cookies, HTTP Basic, client certificates, and mixed authentication chains.
- REST and stateless are not sufficient reasons by themselves.
- Separate security chains can apply the correct policy to different parts of one application.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
CSRF protection can be disabled for an endpoint only when that endpoint cannot be authenticated by a credential the browser sends automatically. A common example is a bearer-only API: client code must add the token to the `Authorization` header, so a cross-site form arrives without an accepted credential.

CSRF must remain enabled when the endpoint accepts a session cookie, a JWT cookie, HTTP Basic authentication, a client certificate, or another ambient credential. Calling an endpoint REST or stateless does not answer the security question. Basic authentication, for example, can be stateless while the browser still resends the credential.

In Spring Security I would apply the decision to a specific `SecurityFilterChain` after checking all of its authentication mechanisms. A mixed application can keep CSRF for browser pages and use a separate bearer-only chain for `/api/**`. If a cookie-authenticated request gets a CSRF 403, the correct fix is to submit the expected token rather than disable the protection.
